lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 2020, four children on a beach in Arctic Norway found a tiny wooden boat. Inside were postcards, still dry.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: They had been sent by the ocean, from an island off Scotland more than a thousand miles away.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: This is St Kilda. For most of the year, no ship could reach it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 1877, a journalist stuck there with nine shipwrecked sailors threw a message into the sea, tied to a lifebuoy.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Nine days later, it washed up in Orkney. A ship came to rescue them.

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: Nine days. My parcels take longer than that.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 1885, a storm ruined the island's food. A fourteen-year-old boy carved five little boats, and sent them out asking for help.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: One of them reached the Isle of Lewis. The newspapers picked up the story, and a relief boat came.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: After that, it became the island's mail. A carved boat, a sheepskin float, the letters sealed in a tin, launched when the wind blew from the northwest.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: About two out of every three were found, in Scotland or in Norway.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In 1930, the last thirty-six islanders left St Kilda for good.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Eighty years later, the National Trust for Scotland launched one more mailboat, with seven postcards.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: It drifted for ten years, all the way to that beach in Norway. And the postcards got delivered. Subscribe for more.
